H2 unknown, with fair hints in E3 (manager says remote staff mostly joined recently) and E4 (18-month rule). H3 contradicted from E1. H4 unknown. H5 unknown. case.title: Remote promotion gap at Fenwright Data Services
case.setting: Fenwright Data Services is a fictional data-services company with about 1,100 employees across two offices, Larkhaven and Calderbrook, plus a fully remote workforce. Promotions are decided in one annual cycle: managers nominate and a Promotion Committee of directors approves or defers nominations. The FY2026 cycle closed in September 2026, and the People Analytics dashboard shows remote employees promoted at less than half the rate of office-based employees.
case.presentingRequest: The COO has asked the People team to confirm by Friday that proximity bias explains the remote promotion gap, so the executive team can announce a rule that employees must work from an office at least three days a week to be considered for promotion. You have been asked to say what is driving the gap and what the company should do.

initialEvidence.text: Promotion dashboard, FY2026 cycle (census 31 Aug 2026; decisions effective 1 Oct 2026). Promotion rate = promotions divided by headcount at census. Office-based (including hybrid): 122 of 760 (16.1%). Remote: 26 of 340 (7.6%). By job family: Engineering, office 61/380 (16.1%), remote 14/170 (8.2%). Customer Operations, office 33/220 (15.0%), remote 7/110 (6.4%). Sales & Account Management, office 28/160 (17.5%), remote 5/60 (8.3%). Automated dashboard flag: 'Remote promotion rate below office rate in every job family.'

initialEvidence.source: Email from Danica Ferrol, Chief Operating Officer, to the executive team
initialEvidence.text: Subject: Remote promotion gap. 'The dashboard could not be clearer. Remote staff are promoted at under half the office rate, in every job family. This is proximity bias, plain and simple: people who aren't in the room don't get seen. I propose that from the FY2027 cycle, anyone who wants to be considered for promotion works from an office at least three days a week. I know roughly 180 of our remote people live more than 150 km from Larkhaven or Calderbrook and were hired on home-based contracts, but if they want to progress they need to be visible. Can the People team confirm the diagnosis by Friday so we can announce?'

initialEvidence.source: HR business partner interview notes, 15 Oct 2026
initialEvidence.text: Engineering manager (Larkhaven, team of 11, 5 remote): 'When an urgent client escalation comes in I'll usually hand it to whoever's sitting near me. It's quicker. I suppose that's the kind of work that gets noticed at promotion time.' Customer Operations manager (Calderbrook, team of 14, 6 remote): 'None of my remote people were put forward this year. Honestly, they're solid. Most of them haven't been with us long, and I didn't have a remote person I could make a case for yet.' Neither manager could say how many stretch assignments each team member had received this year.

initialEvidence.source: Fenwright Promotion Policy v4 (effective January 2024), section 3
initialEvidence.text: Section 3, Eligibility. 3.1 To be nominated in an annual cycle, an employee must have at least 18 months in their current level at the census date and a most recent performance rating of 'Meets' or above. 3.2 Managers nominate. The Promotion Committee approves or defers each nomination. 3.3 Exception nominations for employees with under 18 months in level require a director's written justification and are expected to be rare. 3.4 Work location is recorded on the nomination packet for administrative purposes.

Response rate: remote 71%, office-based 64%. 'I understand what I need to do to be promoted here': agree, remote 41%, office-based 58%. 'Senior leaders are aware of my work': agree, remote 33%, office-based 47%. 'My manager supports my career development': agree, remote 72%, office-based 70%. 'I have the tools I need to do my job well': agree, remote 81%, office-based 79%. Results are reported by work arrangement only; no breakdown by tenure is available in the survey tool.

Not eligible 200, exception nominations 6, approved 4 (2.0%). Remote: eligible 110, nominated 31 (28.2%), approved 22 (71.0% of nominees; 20.0% of eligible). Not eligible 230, exception nominations 6, approved 4 (1.7%). Share of headcount eligible: office 73.7%, remote 32.4%. Applying office within-band rates to the remote eligibility mix gives an expected remote rate of 8.2%, against the observed 7.6%. Analyst note: the eligible-band difference of 1.1 points rests on 110 remote employees. It could be chance, and these data cannot rule out a true difference of several points in either direction.

catalogue.text: Remote hiring was opened to all roles in July 2024. Before that, remote work required an individual exception. Remote employees at 31 Aug 2026: 340. Start dates: before July 2024, 61; July 2024 to February 2025, 64; March 2025 to August 2026, 215. Office-based employees at 31 Aug 2026: 760, of whom 120 started in March 2025 or later. Voluntary exits in the 12 months to 31 Aug 2026: remote 31 (10.9% of average headcount 285); office-based 88 (11.6% of average headcount 757). First-year voluntary exit rate: remote 14.2%, office-based 15.0%. Transfers between arrangements since July 2024: 22 office-to-remote, 3 remote-to-office.

catalogue.title: Performance rating distribution by work arrangement, 2026 mid-year review
catalogue.text: Five-point scale. Among rated employees: 'Meets' or above, remote 87%, office-based 88%. 'Exceeds' or above, remote 24%, office-based 27%. 'Below' or lower, remote 4%, office-based 3%. Employees with under six months' service at the review date are not rated: remote 92, office-based 41. Ratings are entered by line managers and moderated within each job family. No calibration adjustment by work arrangement was recorded.

catalogue.title: Promotion Committee calibration minutes, FY2026 cycle
catalogue.text: The committee of six directors met 9 to 11 September 2026 and reviewed 203 nominations, including 12 exception nominations. 148 were approved and 55 were not approved, 14 of them recorded as 'insufficient evidence of scope'. Packets include the manager's case, rating history, level, time in level and work location. Reasons are recorded per case, but outcomes are not tallied by location. One director commented that 'remote cases tended to be thinner on cross-team examples'. The chair noted that this had not been checked.

catalogue.title: Promotion nomination form template and manager guidance, 2026
catalogue.text: The nomination form has four sections: scope evidence, impact examples, peer feedback and a readiness statement. The guidance asks managers to 'include at least two cross-team examples' and to keep the case under 1,200 words. Level, time in level, latest rating and work location are filled in automatically from HRIS. The guidance has not changed since the 2024 cycle apart from a new deadline date.

catalogue.title: Office badge-access records for office-based staff, January to August 2026
catalogue.text: Office-based staff averaged 3.2 badge days per week (Larkhaven 3.4, Calderbrook 2.9). 14% of hybrid staff averaged fewer than one badge day per week. Attendance peaks on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Records cover only employees assigned to an office and include no remote staff. The extract was not linked to promotion, rating or nomination data.

catalogue.title: Base-pay position within salary band by work arrangement, 2026 pay review
catalogue.text: Median compa-ratio (base pay divided by band midpoint): remote 0.97, office-based 0.99. Under the offer guidelines, remote new hires since 2025 were placed at 0.95 on average. Pay is not location-adjusted within the country. The 2026 merit budget was 3.5% for both groups. The review found no band breaches and made no recommendations on work arrangement.

catalogue.title: Free-text comments from remote respondents, June 2026 engagement pulse
catalogue.source: Survey vendor export (214 comments; selection shown)
catalogue.text: 'You have to be in Larkhaven to get noticed.' 'My manager is great but the directors have never met me.' 'Nobody told me when I was hired that I couldn't go for promotion until I'd been here a year and a half.' 'Office people get the fun client fires.' 'Remote has been fine for my career so far.' 'Visibility is a problem; I'm not sure promotions are.' The selection was chosen by the People team to illustrate themes and is not weighted by frequency.

catalogue.title: Interview with the Promotion Committee chair, 20 October 2026
catalogue.text: 'We judge the case, not the postcode. Location is on the packet because payroll needs it, and nobody looks at it. If remote people aren't getting through, it's because they aren't being nominated, so talk to managers.' When asked for figures, the chair said the committee does not keep approval rates by location. 'I'd be surprised if there's any difference at our stage, but I haven't looked.'

catalogue.title: Industry report on promotion outcomes for remote workers, 2026
catalogue.text: Across 41 participating employers (anonymised), fully remote employees were promoted at 0.69 times the rate of office-based peers. The report attributes the gap to 'visibility deficits' and markets a visibility-coaching product. Methodology note: rates are raw promotions divided by headcount, with no adjustment for tenure, level or role. Participating employers self-selected, and Fenwright is not among them.

catalogue.title: Learning-platform course completions by work arrangement, January to August 2026
catalogue.text: Average course completions per employee: remote 6.1, office-based 4.8. Mandatory compliance modules: 97% completion in both groups. Enrolment in the leadership-track programme: remote 9%, office-based 11%. Completion data are not linked to promotion records. The platform team notes that onboarding courses inflate completion counts for recent joiners.

catalogue.title: Reporting lines and manager span of control by work arrangement
catalogue.text: Of 340 remote employees, 221 (65%) report to office-based managers and 119 to remote managers. Average span of control: office-based managers 8.1 direct reports, remote managers 7.6. Average number of manager changes in the past 12 months: remote 0.3, office-based 0.3. This extract does not include promotion, nomination or rating outcomes by manager location.

catalogue.title: Project staffing records by work arrangement, January to August 2026
catalogue.text: Records project codes and hours booked per employee. Average concurrent projects: remote 2.3, office-based 2.4. The 'role on project' field, intended to flag lead or stretch roles, is blank on 71% of records. Client-escalation work is booked to a general support code and is not attributed to individuals. People Analytics comment: 'This system cannot tell us who received stretch or high-visibility work.'

catalogue.title: FY2025 promotion cycle summary by work arrangement
catalogue.text: FY2025 cycle, census 31 Aug 2025. Promotion rate = promotions divided by headcount at census. Office-based: 113 of 731 (15.5%). Remote: 17 of 181 (9.4%). The report comments that 'the remote gap warrants attention' and recommends that leadership 'monitor visibility'. No breakdown by level, tenure or job family was produced, and no follow-up analysis was commissioned.

catalogue.title: Office space utilisation report, Larkhaven and Calderbrook, 2026
catalogue.text: Larkhaven: 520 desks, average daily occupancy 61%, peak 84% on Wednesdays. Calderbrook: 300 desks, average daily occupancy 55%, peak 77%. The report estimates that an extra 180 regular attenders at three days a week could be absorbed at Larkhaven only by reintroducing desk booking. The Calderbrook lease renewal is due in 2027.

hypotheses.text: The remote–office promotion gap arises because managers and the Promotion Committee favour employees they work alongside in person.
The remote–office promotion gap arises because remote employees, as a group, have spent less time in their current level than office-based employees, not because of where they work.
The remote–office promotion gap arises because remote employees are concentrated in job families that offer fewer promotions.
Remote employees are offered fewer stretch or high-visibility assignments than comparable office-based employees.
The remote–office promotion gap arises because remote employees leave the company at a higher rate, so fewer of them stay long enough to be considered for promotion.

edges.to: Lower chance of promotion in the FY2026 cycle

edges.from: Fewer months in current level at the census date
edges.to: Lower chance of promotion in the FY2026 cycle

actions.text: Adopt the COO's proposal: from the FY2027 cycle, require at least three office days a week for any employee to be considered for promotion.
Put the attendance proposal on hold, and change promotion reporting to compare remote and office-based employees who were eligible under the policy, then re-check that comparison at the FY2027 cycle.
Replace manager-assigned stretch work with a centrally posted, application-based process to correct remote employees' reduced access to it.
Run briefings for remote employees that explain the promotion criteria and eligibility rules.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: Fenwright opened all roles to remote hiring in July 2024. As a result, 215 of its 340 remote employees started in March 2025 or later, so at the FY2026 census they had less than the 18 months in level that the promotion policy requires. Only 32.4% of remote employees were eligible, against 73.7% of office-based employees. Among eligible employees, nomination rates (28.2% vs 28.6%), committee approval rates (71.0% vs 73.8%) and promotion rates (20.0% vs 21.1%) are nearly identical. Applying office within-band rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, close to the observed 7.6%. So the raw 8.5-point gap comes from differences in time in level, not from work location. Job-family mix is the same in both groups, and the gap appears within each family, so job family does not explain it. Voluntary attrition is no higher among remote staff (10.9% vs 11.6%), so the shorter time in level reflects recent hiring, not churn. The association between working remotely and promotion is real but confounded. The within-band sample is too small to rule out a small direct effect, and too small to show one. The COO's proximity-bias diagnosis and the promotion-linked attendance rule rest on raw rates. That rule would effectively bar about 180 home-based employees from promotion without addressing anything that drives the gap. Whether remote staff get fewer stretch assignments remains untested, because no system records that work.

answers.rationale: C1 shows near-identical nomination and approval rates for eligible remote and office-based employees. Differences in eligibility mix account for about 7.9 of the 8.5-point raw gap (expected 8.2% vs observed 7.6%). Favouritism by managers or the committee is therefore not what produces the gap. E3's anecdote, C4's director comment and C10's industry figure are unadjusted or anecdotal and do not outweigh C1.

E4 makes 18 months in level a gate for nomination. C1 shows 67.6% of remote employees below the threshold against 26.3% of office-based employees, with promotion rates within each band almost equal across arrangements. C2 explains the pattern: remote hiring opened in July 2024. C1 is required because only within-band rates rule out H1 as the rival explanation.

E1 shows the same job-family mix in both groups (Engineering 50% vs 50%, Customer Operations 32% vs 29%, Sales 18% vs 21%). The gap of roughly half persists within every family, so job-family mix cannot explain it.

The only evidence is one manager's account of handing escalations to people sitting nearby (E3) and unweighted survey comments (C8). C13 states that no system records who receives stretch or high-visibility work. C1 concerns promotion outcomes, not assignment access. The claim is live but unestablished.

C1 shows that remote employees have less time in level but cannot say whether that comes from churn or recent hiring. C2 settles it: remote voluntary attrition (10.9%) and first-year attrition (14.2%) are no higher than office-based rates (11.6%, 15.0%), and 215 of 340 remote employees started in March 2025 or later. The shortfall reflects recent hiring, not departures.

The raw association is real and recurs across years (E1, C14). C1 shows that time in level accounts for it, so causation is not established. The C1 analyst note says the within-band data on 110 remote employees cannot rule out a true difference of several points either way, so the evidence does not count decisively against any effect. The edge is association-only, not contradicted.

Time in level precedes the cycle. E4 documents a formal eligibility gate that explains the mechanism. C1 shows the same steep difference (about 20–21% vs about 2%) inside both work arrangements, so location is ruled out as the main rival.
C2 shows equal or slightly lower voluntary attrition among remote staff, both overall and in the first year. The evidence counts against the link itself, not merely in favour of a rival.

E2 acknowledges that about 180 remote employees live more than 150 km from an office and were hired on home-based contracts. The rule would effectively bar them from promotion. Under the supported explanation (C1), it targets a factor that is not driving the gap. Even under the proximity-bias rival, it would penalise the employees rather than the bias. It causes damage under every live hypothesis.

C1 shows the headline metric is confounded by eligibility mix. Holding the proposal prevents harm, and reporting within eligibility bands gives leadership the correct comparison. Re-checking at FY2027 covers the small-sample uncertainty in the within-band gap. A2 is the only action that addresses the pending decision and the faulty metric.

A3 is justified only if H4 is true, and H4 is unknown: there is one anecdote, and C13 shows no data exist. If H4 were confirmed, a posted process would clearly help. If H4 is wrong, the cost is reversible administrative overhead. Committing now is not justified.

E5 shows remote employees are less clear on what is needed for promotion (41% vs 58%), and C8 includes a remote joiner unaware of the 18-month rule. A briefing is reasonable and low-risk. It does not address the pending attendance decision or the misleading metric, so it is not among the best actions.

The highest-ranked action, A2, is substantive: it declines the attendance rule and changes reporting. C1 shows the gap is accounted for by eligibility mix, and C2 confirms the composition comes from recent hiring. That is enough to commit to a low-risk, reversible decision, and A2 already includes a re-check for the residual uncertainty.

truth.authoringNotes: Initial-file-only answers: H1 tempting as supported, careful answer unknown. H2 unknown, with fair hints in E3 (manager says remote staff mostly joined recently) and E4 (18-month rule). H3 contradicted from E1. H4 unknown. H5 unknown. R1 association-only (naive answer: causal). R3 unknown. A2 cannot yet be ranked preferred. SUFF insufficient. Only C1 provides within-band nomination, approval and promotion rates, so only C1 settles H1, H2, A2 and SUFF. Only C2 provides attrition and hiring dates, so only C2 settles H5 and R3. A wrong pair such as C1+C4 or C2+C9 therefore loses points. Misleading distractors: C4 (a director's unchecked comment), C9 (an interested chair with no data), C10 (vendor raw rates with a product to sell), C14 (a repeat of the raw gap), C8 (curated comments). C3 and C13 are reasonable requests that do not move any key. Under the edge-semantics tension, R1 is keyed association-only because C1 explicitly cannot rule out a few-point effect, whereas H1 is keyed contradicted because it claims the gap arises from favouritism, and composition accounts for about 93% of the gap with matched nomination and approval rates. Arithmetic check: 61+33+28=122; 14+7+5=26; 118+4=122; 22+4=26; nominations 160+6+31+6=203; approvals 148; 0.324×21.1+0.676×2.0≈8.2%.
